results.title: Alerts should follow best practices, be actionable, have realistic thresholds, a relevant description and clear resolution path
results.body_snippet:
### Enhancement Proposal

Some alerts in Grafana Agent charm are not a symptom of an actual issue in the systems and services being monitored, but only indicate some systems metrics have an unexpected value from a very specific perspective that might not match the actual use case for the system.

This is not a good practice to define such alerts, even as warnings (as the thresholds are not configurable), as they only lead to alert fatigue and are rarely actionable, having no clear path to resolution.

Alerts should be based on metrics related to an actual degraded end-user experience or system/service failure. Failing to do so will overload an operational team with alerts that will only get disregarded as noise over time, distracting operators from actual problems that require their attention.

Could you please remove these alerts? (list is not exhaustive, more might not be relevant to actual problems):
- HostMemory
- HostMemoryFull
- HostSwapFull
- ProcessesIncresingWarning

- HostLoggedInUsers
- RaidDisksSpare

results.title: [6.1] Cron run "failed" notifications fire during hot reload and during retries, causing alert fatigue
results.body_snippet:
## 1. Environment

- OpenClaw version: 2026.6.1 (latest stable on npm dist-tag `latest`)
- Upgraded from: 2026.5.12 (5.12) where this issue did not exist
- Provider: an anthropic-messages-compatible LLM endpoint (M2.7 + M3 model endpoints, both via `minimax` provider alias)
- Channel: Feishu (1 bot account)
- Cron workload: ~30 cron jobs (5-minute to daily schedules), 2 isolated lane worker pool

## 2. Summary

After upgrading from OpenClaw 5.12 to 6.1, cron run failure notifications became noisy. Investigation shows that **most "failed" notifications are false positives** — the actual isolated session is still running and completes minutes later, posting a second "completed" notification in the same scheduling window.

The pattern is consistent with **three 5.26-introduced mechanisms that did not exist in 5.12**:

1. **`cron.retry`** — default `maxAttempts: 3`, `backoffMs: [30000, 60000, 300000]`, `retryOn: [rate_limit, overloaded, network, timeout, server_error]`. In 5.12 there was no retry, a single fail was final.
2. **`auth.cooldowns`** — default `authPermanentBackoffMinutes: 10` after a transient failure. 5.12 had no cooldown concept.
3. **Config hot reload on mtime change**

results.title: False positive: CVE-2024-3566 (Windows-only) incorrectly reported on Linux-based containers
results.body_snippet:
### Current Behavior

Dependency-Track reports [CVE-2024-3566](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-3566) as affecting PHP components (e.g., `php@8.2.18`) used in Linux-based Docker containers (such as Alpine Linux).

However, this CVE is **specific to Windows environments**, due to its reliance on backslash (`\`) path traversal behavior, which is **not valid or exploitable on POSIX systems** like Linux.

The NVD explicitly includes the following CPE constraint:
`Running on/with`
`cpe:2.3:o:microsoft:windows:-:*:*:*:*:*:*:*`

Despite this, Dependency-Track applies the CVE to any project/component using a matching PHP version, **regardless of the actual operating system**, which leads to false positives for environments that will never be affected.

This appears to be caused by the fact that **Dependency-Track does not evaluate CPE platform constraints (like the OS)** when matching CVEs with components.

Currently, updating filters across multiple dashboard components and alerts is a manual, fragmented process. When teams need to modify filter criteria, they must remember to update each individual widget and alert separately. This scattered approach leads to:

results.title: Ability to mark a vulnerability as only impacting certain release artifacts
results.body_snippet:
Hi, @woodruffw suggested I file this here, since the Python vulnerability data uses the osv schema.

I'm one of the maintainers of the popular python `cryptography` package. We ship both source ("sdist") and binary ("wheel") artifacts for all of our releases.

Our binary wheels include a statically linked copy of OpenSSL. This copy may be impacted by upstream OpenSSL security issues.

We'd like to mark our package as impacted by these, so users are aware. _However_, our source packages are _not_ impacted by these, since they don't include a copy of OpenSSL -- they link against the system OpenSSL. If we simply mark a vulnerability as impacting our package, it'll generate false positives for any source users, contributing to alert fatigue.

We'd therefore like some sort of additional metadata to specify that only some artifacts are impacted by a given vulnerability.

## Problem

When two regional MeshCore meshes get **bridged** (intentionally or accidentally), observers in one region start seeing adverts from nodes with GPS coordinates in a completely different region. Today, the ingestor **silently drops** these out-of-region adverts via `NodePassesGeoFilter()` ([main.go L311](cmd/ingestor/main.go#L311)). This means:

1. **No visibility** — operators don't know bridging is happening
2. **Data loss** — foreign adverts are discarded, not logged
3. **No forensics** — can't determine when bridging started, which nodes are entry points, or whether it's intentional

Operators need to know when this is happening and which nodes are the bridge entry points.

- `internal/geofilter/` provides `PassesFilter()` — polygon + buffer zone check

- Nodes without GPS (`0,0`) pass through (correct — can't classify them)

results.title: Reduce False Positives in Drowsiness Detection
results.body_snippet:
## Summary

DICE includes a computer vision-based drowsiness detection system designed to monitor user alertness through facial landmarks and eye state analysis.

While the current implementation is functional, it may occasionally generate false positives or incorrect drowsiness alerts under certain real-world conditions.

This issue aims to improve the reliability, robustness, and overall accuracy of the drowsiness detection pipeline.

---

## Current Behavior

The existing system can incorrectly classify users as drowsy in situations such as:

- Normal blinking.
- Looking down at the keyboard.
- Looking away from the screen.
- Poor lighting conditions.
- Users wearing glasses.
- Temporary face occlusions.
- Variations in camera angle or distance.

These false detections reduce the overall user experience and may cause unnecessary interruptions.

---

## Expected Behavior

The drowsiness detection system should distinguish genuine signs of fatigue from normal user behavior.

The assistant should:

- Reduce false positive alerts.
- Remain reliable under varying lighting conditions.
- Handle different camera positions and user distances.
- Continue functioning for users with glasses

results.body_snippet:
# What 

SniffCheck is flagging normal Wi-Fi networks as evil twins.

Current logic: Same SSID + multiple BSSID/vendor = Evil Twin Suspect

But the same SSID with more than one BSSID/vendor could be normal. Mesh systems, extenders, ISP routers, and office APs all do this.

So SniffCheck is being too aggressive. 

## Why it matters

We know SniffCheck is not going to catch someone who really knows what they are doing every time.

That is not the point.

The hope is that SniffCheck can still help someone avoid getting got by a script kiddy running a basic evil twin setup.

For that to work, the warning needs to be trusted.

If normal Wi-Fi networks keep getting flagged, users will ignore the alert when it actually matters.

results.title: DL3064 - False positives in sensitive variable check due to simple substring matching (e.g. GOPRIVATE)
results.body_snippet:
## Problem
ref. https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint/pull/1188

The current implementation of `DL3064` relies on naive substring matching (`suspiciousSubstrings`). This causes high-volume false positives for standard ecosystem variables, public identifiers, and harmless build metadata.

Here are a few examples.
- `GOPRIVATE` (Go module proxy pattern, not a credential).
- `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE` (Standard variable for AWS EKS IRSA authentication).
- `TRAVIS_OS_NAME` (build OS), `TRAVIS_SUDO` (boolean flag), and `FACEBOOK_APP_ID` (public client identifier).

results.title: Measure and publish the false-positive rate on normal traffic
results.body_snippet:
## Why

This is the highest-value missing number in the whole project, and almost no student IDS project has it.

ML-based intrusion detection does not fail in the real world because accuracy is too low. It fails because of alert fatigue: a 0.5% false-positive rate on a busy link is thousands of junk alerts a day, so operators mute it. `CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD` currently defaults to 0.85 and `ANOMALY_THRESHOLD` to 0.7 with no stated justification for either.

## Tasks

- [ ] Capture roughly an hour of ordinary traffic on your own machine with no attacks running
- [ ] Run detection over it and count alerts. Every alert is by definition a false positive
- [ ] Report false positives per hour at the default thresholds
- [ ] Sweep the confidence threshold and plot a precision-recall curve

- A stated figure of the form "N false positives/hour at threshold T"
- A committed precision-recall curve

results.title: session-guard: routing check false-positives on ANTHROPIC_MODEL=opus (benign model selection)
results.body_snippet:
## Summary

The `session-guard` **routing guard** raises a `ROUTING OVERRIDE` alert whenever a fleet agent's live process has `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` set — regardless of its value. But `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` merely *selects* a model; a value like `opus` (or any `claude-*` id) is the fleet's normal Anthropic path, not a reroute. The result is a persistent **false positive**: on a normally-configured Opus fleet, the guard fires `ROUTING OVERRIDE on 'main': ... ANTHROPIC_MODEL=opus` on **every sweep**, indefinitely.

## Impact

Alert fatigue, and the bad kind — the guard exists to catch a genuine security event (an agent silently rerouted off Anthropic, per the 2026-07-15 incident), but by crying wolf every ~15 min for days it trains the operator to ignore the very channel a real reroute would arrive on. In one run it fired dozens of times across several days while the config was completely benign.

## Root cause

`bin/session-guard`, live-process routing check (~line 101):

```sh
for var in ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL ANTHROPIC_MODEL ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; do
  val=$(... "$var" ...)
  [ -n "$val" ] || continue
  ... alert_main "routing-$ws" "ROUTING OVERRIDE ... $var=$val ..."
done
```

results.title: Track operational metrics, not only ROC-AUC
results.body_snippet:
## Summary
The current evaluation story still over-emphasizes headline metrics like ROC-AUC, even though the practical problem is alert fatigue from false positives.

## Why this matters
For anomaly detection, a decent ROC-AUC can still produce an unusable alert stream. The project already notes that thousands of false positives make the tool hard to use in practice.

## Proposed changes
- Add evaluation outputs for:
  - precision-recall AUC
  - false positives per hour on benign-only captures
  - recall at a fixed false-positive budget
  - top-K precision for analyst triage / CTF workflows
- Choose thresholds from operational constraints rather than ROC-optimal cutoffs alone.
- Record these metrics in the exported model bundle manifest.
- Update README results reporting to emphasize operational metrics over a single AUC number.

## Acceptance criteria
- Training/evaluation pipeline reports PR-AUC and at least one false-positive-budget metric.
- Threshold selection is configurable by an operational target, not only by ROC heuristics.
